newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW - Baer sees risk, also gains in equities.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Baer sees risk, also gains in equities.

text.p: Swiss private bank Julius Baer, with managed assets in excess of 56 billion Swiss francs, still sees scope for gains in equity markets but has lately favoured a strategy of buying convertible bonds in the U.S. to cut risk.

"If you sum up the bond strategy, we are certainly not interested in Japanese bonds. But we believe U.S. bond yields are no longer rising, which is a positive for the rest of the world, not only for bonds but also for equities," said Otto Waser, Baer's chief investment strategist, in an interview.
He said it had become harder to find stocks offering significant upside potential after such strong gains.
In some markets, including the U.S. and the Far East, Baer is buying convertible bonds to mitigate risk.
"Buying the convertible bond gives you participation on the upside and gives you some downside protection," he said.
The bonds offer protection similar to stock options.
One issue Baer currently recommends to non-U.S. investors is a convertible bond by Thermo Instrument Systems, issued October 10, 1996, and maturing in 2003.
In Asian stock markets, Waser noted the trend is far less uniform than three years ago.

"It is a heterogeneous region. It is not a one-way market. A lot of economies are in trouble. Thailand's market has lost nearly half its value in three years, while Hong Kong has managed to gain new highs," he said.

In the U.S. Baer began to see prospects for slower growth as early as July, following Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony. It will continue to watch the situation there in the future.
Baer manages roughly 70 percent of the assets for private clients and the remainder for institutional clients.
For higher-risk U.S.-dollar based private clients, it currently allocates about 35 percent of its dollar holdings to fixed-income, and 15 percent of assets to equities.
Waser is more optimistic about prospects for European stocks than European bonds on a near-term basis, but sees some areas where bonds could still produce favourable returns longer-term.
Five-year Italian government bonds yielded about 7.47 percent on Friday compared with 4.72 percent for five-year Bunds and 3.03 percent for five-year Swiss bonds.
"The Italian bond market is, just for risk-oriented investors, still relatively attractive," Waser said.
He said Baer cut its holdings of lira-denominated bonds, taking profits when the mark/lira cross rate fell towards 1,000.00 lire in late June, but continued to recommend them.
"These markets had a big run in the last two months, but offer some yield-pickup with a long-term view," he added.

German bonds might have topped out, however. "We feel with yields at 6.00 percent, the long end of the German market doesn't offer very good value. It is also very close to historic lows so investors are getting more cautious," he said.
Overall, he sees a favourable outlook for European markets.
"In terms of global allocation we are heavily geared towards Europe, because of the monetary environment and prospects for economic and corporate earnings growth," he said.
Waser is optimistic about European markets, believing currencies within Europe which are part of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) are mostly in line with fundamentals.
"We are very close to the central rates in the ERM. We believe that the central rates will give a reasonably good guidance to where the currencies will be fixed in monetary union," he said.

With respect to equities, Waser currently favours Germany, the Netherlands and also selected stocks in France, as well as in the U.K. where Bear sees the market underpinned by corporate earnings growth.
On an individual basis he favours stocks of large concerns with proven track records.
In Switzerland these include Novartis partners Ciba-Geigy AG and Sandoz AG, as well as insurers Swiss Re, Zurich Insurance and Swiss Bank Corp.
